questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That I had the possibility to learn French, and that I could follow a lot of EU law-related courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The only downside is that it can be an administrative hell. It is very stressfull before and after you leave, and you have to fill out a lot of documents and coordinate them between the two universities. It can be difficult to attain all the information you need, and sometimes things will only get solved at the very last minute. But if you can be calm about that, the experience is really worth it!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Very difficult! I wasn't really contacted much by ULB until a couple of days before my classes started. I also came to Brussels early to follow a French course provided by ULB, but in the end I couldn't follow the course, as it was impossible to attain information about it or contact anyone. I also ended up attending a lot of introductory lectures and events, that were only meant for full-time students, which were very confusing and not relevant to me at all, because I did not receive any information about which introductory events I could attend as an Erasmus student. In fact, there weren't really any introductory events for Erasmus students, apart from a single lunch-break meeting halfway into the semester. 
But on the other side, the ULB administration is very helpful and flexible (once you get a hold on them), so they can solve almost any inconvenience resulting from a lack of information on their side.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I could stop by the Erasmus coordinators office and receive a goodie bag with some ULB merchandise and a few letters of information. As far as I remember, I also received a couple of emails, but mostly I had to find information on my own on the ULB website and by asking around.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: No

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy! If you are a Dane, you can apply for a room at the Danish Church, which is both cheaper than most other options, close to ULB, and in a very nice neighborhood. You have to apply early though, as all the rooms get rented out very quickly! It is a very social dorm, and you will live only with other Danes. So if you don't want that, you should apply for a more international dorm. If you don't get a room at the Church, you can also apply for one at "Helenehusene", which are a bit more expensive.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Ixelles is a really nice area with a lot of bars and restaurants, and it is fairly close to ULB!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Information was scarce, and many of the courses I had planned on following, were not available. But on the other hand, the professors and administration were very flexible for us Erasmus students, so they could bend the rules a bit to let us follow different courses.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
First, you have to send a list of the courses you intend to follow (the OLA), which will be available to both KU and ULB. Then, you have to go to the first class of every course and ask the professor for permission to follow the course, as some professors do not want international students on their courses. Most professors were very open, but a few said no, which meant that I had to change my learning agreement last minute. However, KU were very fast at changing my "forhåndsgodkendelse", so it was not a problem. 

You had the opportunity to try out courses for two weeks before having to finally choose which ones to follow, which was very nice.

Also, the exam dates for each course will not be available until late November. This meant that I had two exams at the same time. But luckily the ULB administration and the professors were very flexible in solving this, so they just arranged an oral exam for me instead. So if you have a problem like this, just ask the professor - they will usually be very willing to find another solution, and the system is not as strict as in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not much! I had to find most information on the website.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was mostly successful. Only one or two professors had closed classes, but easily found other courses to substitute them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just keep calm, and remember that you are on exchange to learn how they do things in other countries! Few countries have a bureaucracy as organized as Denmark's, and sometimes you will not be able to get the information you need until the very last minute. But trust that it will all get sorted out in the end.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: They were pretty similar to the level at UCPH, if not a bit easier.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Very different. There were only lectures, and in most classes oral participation at lectures counted towards our final grade. You can also choose to follow "Travaux Pratiques" (TP) for most courses, which are similar to seminar classes in Denmark. These are optional (for most courses), and are an opportunity to go more in depth with the syllabus. I only followed TP for one course, where it was mandatory. It was very time consuming, so I would not recommend it if it is optional. But it helped me a lot towards the final exam, and I also obtained a few points that counted in my final grade.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Public International Law (10 ects)
Decision-making in the EU (5 ects)
EU Criminal Law (5 ects) 
Internal Market with a focus on the Free Movement of Goods (5 ects)
Terrorism and International Law (5 ects)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would really recommend Terrorism and International Law. The professor is very charismatic, and the exam is a paper that you can write after you return to Denmark. This is a relief, as the exams at ULB are mostly hand-written, closed book-exams, which is very different than what we are used to in Denmark.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I went out to eat and drink a lot, as I made some very good friends at my dorm. This was not "unexpected", but I did end up spending a lot more money on food and drinks than I'm used to. We also went on a lot of trips, which were a bit expensive, but really worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was surprised that the cost of living was very similar to what it is in Denmark. Going out to eat and shopping at the supermarket was quite expensive. But coffee to go was very cheap, and books for university were as well!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I didn't have time to join myself, but I heard many good things about ULB Sport, where you can follow all sorts of fitness classes very cheap. There were also a huge number of student organizations, that we were welcome to join (but you would need to speak French).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go on trips with your friends! You can go to Paris by train in 1,5 hour. Also, explore Belgium outside of Brussels - go hiking in the Ardennes, and visit Ghent, Brugge and Leuven.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Grand Place, visit the Africa museum, eat frites and waffles. Go on a day trip to Ghent. Go to cosy cafes such as Chyl, Cafe de la Presse (close to ULB) and Bisou. Try the "beer-o-meter" at Delirium, where you can try a selection of 10 Belgian beers.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy! Much more similar to Copenhagen than I expected, but also with everything that I love about the more southern parts of Europe - farmers markets with fresh fruits and vegetables, a "going out-culture", where people meet with their friends for a glass of wine after work, and warmer weather with more sunlight over the winter.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join a student organization or attend the ESN-parties.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There were not that many cultural differences. If I have to mention one thing, it is the administration which was much slower and less effective than in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The more extroverted culture, where people chat you up at a lecture or a bar.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Keep calm and trust that the administrative things will all fall into place in due time, even though they will test your patience. 
2. Remember to go out and relax - take a break from studying law in Denmark, where you are buried in books all semester. You don't need to do that here! 
3. Be present, and don't go back to Denmark too often. Also, say no to getting too many visits from back home - you'll need the weekends to get to know your new friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything is usually easier if you show up in person and ask, instead of sending emails and calling. ULB can find a solution for almost any problem you have, you just need to ask.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Regaining my passion for studying law, as it had kind of died after a few years of hard studying. Here, I could focus on just studying subjects I found interesting, without having to focus on anything else such as work.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Just attaining all the correct information.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
